description: Six of us from Baku asking: could a Mars colony survive? Our strategy game puts you in charge of a new colony. You split water, food, energy and crew, and handle crises like dust storms and failing life support. Every choice changes the colony’s future, modeled on real NASA data. Omar, Vahid and Sajjad code, Ravan designs, Sahib and Amina research. Looking for a science mind or a storyteller.
summary:
MARS: The Butterfly Effect is a browser game where players design and run a human mission to Mars between 2042 and 2062. Players land a crew at Jezero Crater, scout for underground ice with a rover and a robot companion, and build habitats, greenhouses and power systems. They also have to balance oxygen, water, food, energy and waste in real physical units.

The game answers the Space Mission Design challenge by building the mission on real NASA data. JPL DE424 ephemerides computed with NASA GMAT set the calendar, the radio delay to Earth, communication blackouts and supply-ship launch windows. NASA Mars-GRAM sets the weather and dust storms, and BVAD, MOXIE and Curiosity RAD data shape life support and radiation. Every number shows whether it is observed, demonstrated, a projection or a game-balance value.

The core mechanic is the "butterfly effect": a decision made today can cause a crisis many sols later. This teaches players the systems thinking that real mission planners need, and it applies to sustainability on Earth too. The game runs offline in any browser, so students and classrooms anywhere can explore NASA science through play.
details:
MARS: The Butterfly Effect is a browser game where you build and run a human colony on Mars from 2042 to 2062. Every run opens with a short cinematic. Then your lander sets down in Jezero Crater with a small crew, and the job is simple to say and hard to do: keep everyone alive and grow the settlement. You send a scout robot and the PIPER rover out to hunt for underground ice. You drag and drop buildings into place and give each crew member a job. You keep track of power, water, oxygen, food, CO₂, soil and waste, all in real physical units. You pick crops for each greenhouse, and when you’re ready, you send expeditions past the edge of your territory.

The heart of the game is the butterfly effect. Your policies, building choices and shortcuts don’t hurt you right away. They come back many sols later as a food shortage, a broken machine, damaged land or a sick crew. Before you commit to a choice, the Butterfly Forecast gives you a hint of where it might lead. The Butterfly Index (0–100) tells you how resilient your colony is, and your Colony Level goes up as the settlement matures.

The world runs on NASA data that ships with the game, so you don’t need an internet connection to play:

  • Calendar, communication and supply ships: Earth and Mars positions come from the JPL DE424 ephemeris, computed with NASA GMAT. They decide the date, the radio delay to Earth, blackouts during solar conjunction, how much sunlight reaches the colony, and when the Hohmann launch windows open for supply ships.
  • Weather: NASA Mars-GRAM 2005 gives temperature, pressure and dust at the real landing site. In global dust-storm years, the game replays the 2001 storm that Mars Global Surveyor watched.
  • Mars time: the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm (Mars Sol Date, solar longitude, local solar time).
  • Life support: how much oxygen, water, food and CO₂ each person needs comes from NASA’s BVAD. Oxygen production follows what Perseverance’s MOXIE actually achieved. The soil and farming model draws on lessons from Biosphere 2.
  • Radiation: the surface dose measured by Curiosity’s RAD instrument.

Every number in the game has an evidence label: Observed, Demonstrated, Projection or Game balance. You always know what’s real science and what’s a design choice.

Benefits

  • You learn how Mars missions really work by running one yourself: launch windows, communication delays, dust storms, closed-loop life support, and the constant balancing act between oxygen, water, food and energy.
  • Dry NASA datasets turn into something you can feel. If your power drops in a dust-storm year, it’s because that storm happened in the real data.
  • It builds systems thinking. Every resource is connected to the others, and a quick win today can cost you badly later.
  • It runs offline in any modern browser with nothing to install, so it works in classrooms and places with weak internet.

Intended impact

We want students, teachers and space fans to come away understanding that a decision on Mars, and on Earth too, can matter long after it’s made. The environmental impact and risk system shows pollution, waste and overuse piling up in specific places until they threaten the colony. That ties straight back to sustainability on our own planet. We also hope the game gets young people curious about NASA’s open data and about careers in space.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: JavaScript (React JSX), HTML, CSS, JSON and Markdown for game content, and Python for the data scripts.
  • Frameworks and libraries: React 19, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber and drei (3D graphics), React Three Rapier (physics), postprocessing, zustand (game state), Motion (UI animations) and i18next (multiple languages).
  • NASA tools and data: NASA GMAT R2026a with JPL DE424 ephemerides, NASA MSFC Mars-GRAM 2005, the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm, NASA BVAD, MOXIE, Curiosity RAD, and the JPL/USGS Mars colour mosaic.
  • Quality: 76 automated unit, balance and acceptance tests. Some of them are “bot playthroughs” that check the game rules against the real data. For example, a colony that relies only on solar power loses power in a global dust-storm year, but one with a reactor doesn’t.
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub, with each of us on our own branch and changes merged through pull requests. We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code and Google Antigravity) with a shared set of rules.
  • Hardware: nothing special. It runs in a normal browser on any laptop.

What makes it creative

  • Most space games use data as decoration. In ours, the NASA data is the game. The calendar, the weather, supply flights and life support all come straight from real models.
  • Making the butterfly effect the core mechanic turns delayed consequences into the challenge, instead of the usual instant reward or punishment.
  • Story and gameplay work together: an opening cinematic, a crew with real roles, a colony radio feed, a mystery storyline, a robot scout companion and a tutorial that coaches you along.
  • Putting an evidence label on every number is an unusual and honest way to deal with scientific accuracy in a game.

What our team had to think about

  • Scientific accuracy vs. fun: we used real data wherever it existed and clearly marked the values we set for game balance. We also wrote down the known limits. Ice-deposit locations are generated for gameplay because the dataset has no map of subsurface ice, and Mars-GRAM runs colder at night than what Perseverance measured.
  • Accessibility: offline play, no API keys, no installation, a guided tutorial and support for several languages.
  • Performance: optimized 3D scenes and a static build, so it runs even on modest computers.
  • Education: short science cards explain the real system behind each mechanic.
  • Sustainability: an environmental impact and risk system, so a growing colony has ecological costs you can see.
  • Teamwork: a shared folder structure, a design-token UI system, game content stored as data files and pull-request reviews. That let two people (and their AI assistants) work at the same time without getting in each other’s way.
